opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's somewhat counterintuitive, because search on the web has been around for twenty-five years and it feels like a solved problem. But I think it was solved for a very specific customer, which is a human sitting in front of a screen.

When you design search for a human, you're optimizing for a lot of constraints that come from human attention. People type two or three words. They look at maybe the first few results. They're not going to read fifty pages. So the whole system is built around guessing intent from a tiny query, ranking ten blue links really well, and keeping the experience fast enough that someone doesn't get bored. A lot of the hard problems in search were really about compensating for how little information the user gives you and how little effort they're willing to spend.

Agents change almost every one of those assumptions. An agent can express what it wants in a long, precise, detailed way. It can say, "I'm looking for companies that do this, in this region, with these characteristics, and I need evidence for each claim." It doesn't get tired. It's happy to read a hundred pages if that gets it a better answer. It can take thirty seconds or a few minutes if the task warrants it. So the problem moves from "guess what this person meant from three words and give them ten links" to "here's a well-specified information need, go do the work and return the right tokens."

That's more tractable because the ambiguity goes down and the budget goes up. You can trade compute for quality in a way you never could with humans. You can do multiple hops, verify things, cross-reference sources, and return structured, cited output instead of a ranked list. And the evaluation becomes clearer too, because the agent has a downstream task, so you can actually measure whether the information helped it succeed, rather than relying on proxies like clicks.

The other piece is that the web itself was never really designed for machines to consume, and the search stack was built around ads and human browsing behavior. When your customer is an agent, you can rethink the index, the ranking, even what a "result" is, from first principles. So in a weird way, the existence of agents takes a problem that felt saturated and reopens it, but on terms that are much more favorable to building something dramatically better.

r001.rationale: The response says search was optimized for humans, then explains that agents change the assumptions and become the customer, making search more tractable through more precise requests and greater capacity to process information.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is actually one of the more counterintuitive things, and it comes from having spent a long time working on search for humans.

Search for humans is really hard because the human on the other side is impatient, and they're not very good at telling you what they want. Someone types three words into a box. Those three words are a very lossy compression of what's actually in their head. So you spend an enormous amount of effort on query understanding, on guessing intent, on personalization, on ranking, because you have to get it right on the first page, ideally the first result. People don't scroll. They don't reformulate. They won't tell you why the result was wrong. And then on top of that you need to render it in a way that a human can skim in two seconds. So the whole product is this very narrow pipe where you have to be nearly perfect at inference and nearly perfect at presentation, with almost no feedback.

An agent flips most of those constraints. First, the agent can actually articulate what it wants. It doesn't give you three words, it can give you a paragraph. It can tell you what it already knows, what it's trying to accomplish, what it's ruled out. So the query understanding problem, which was most of the difficulty, largely goes away. You're not guessing intent anymore, you're being told.

Second, the agent is patient. It's happy to look at twenty results, or a hundred. It doesn't need the best answer at position one, it needs good coverage somewhere in the set, and it will do the reading. That means recall matters a lot more than precision in the old sense, and recall is a much easier problem than exact ranking.

Third, it iterates. If the first set of results is bad, the agent reformulates, tries a different angle, drills in, and it does that in milliseconds without getting frustrated. So search becomes a conversation with a tool rather than a one-shot bet. Each round gives you more signal about what's actually needed.

And fourth, you don't have to worry about the presentation layer nearly as much. You don't need snippets and titles and ten blue links tuned for a human eye. You can return raw passages, structured data, whatever is most useful for a model to consume. A lot of the product complexity just disappears.

So in some ways it's the search problem with the two hardest parts removed: understanding an underspecified human, and making a single perfect choice for them. What's left is more like a retrieval problem in the classic information retrieval sense, which we're actually pretty good at, and which gets better as the models on both ends get better. The place where it gets hard again is freshness and scale and trust, like how do you keep an index of the live web that's good enough for an agent to rely on. But that's an engineering problem more than an inference problem, and I'd much rather have that one.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts search for human users with search for agents and explains that agents can state their needs, tolerate broad result sets, iterate, and consume raw data, making the search problem more tractable.

astra-6.text:
I think agents change what you need to optimize search for. When a human searches, you’re trying to infer a lot from a very short query: what they’re trying to accomplish, what they already know, and what kind of answer would be useful. And you have to get it right quickly, because the human has limited patience for looking through results and trying again.

An agent can make that process explicit. It has context about the task, it can break the task into smaller questions, and it can look at a result and decide, “That didn’t give me what I needed. Let me try a different query.” So search doesn’t have to solve the whole problem in one shot. It becomes a tool inside an iterative process.

That doesn’t make finding reliable information easy. But it gives you a clearer interface: retrieve useful evidence for a specific question, and let the agent use that evidence to figure out the next step. That’s a more tractable problem than trying to anticipate a person’s entire intent from a few words.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts human search needs with agent needs and describes search as a tool agents use iteratively to retrieve evidence for specific questions, clearly presenting agents as a distinct user of search.

sol-6.1.text:
I think agents change what you need to optimize for. When you build search for a human, you’re trying to anticipate exactly what they want and put the right answer in the first few results. The human has limited time and patience, so a lot has to go right in that one interaction.

An agent can make several searches, look at the results, refine the question, and follow up on what’s missing. So the search system doesn’t have to solve the entire problem in one shot. It needs to provide useful evidence that lets the agent make progress.

That also lets you separate retrieval from presentation. You don’t necessarily need a beautifully composed answer from every search. You need relevant information, enough context to interpret it, and a way to go deeper. Search is still hard, but it becomes a more focused problem within a larger reasoning process.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts search built for humans with search used by agents, describing agents as a distinct search user whose iterative searches make the problem more tractable.
